newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African interest rates to stay high -Old Mutual.
newsitem.headline: S.African interest rates to stay high -Old Mutual.

text.p: South African interest rates will stay high into next year and there is a short-term risk of a further hike in the cost of borrowing, the country's leading life assurance group Old Mutual said on Thursday.
"In the short term there is a growing risk that rates could rise," chief economist Dave Mohr said.
South Africa's protracted current account deficit problems, due to booming imports, ruled out any early cut in rates which remain at record real levels, after allowing for inflation.
But despite the high cost of money, Mohr said South Africa should be able to avoid recession. However, next year growth would slow to two percent after a forecast 3.3 percent for 1996.
"By 1998 the economy should be accelerating again, spurred by a healthier global environment, the more competitive exchange rate and, hopefully, lower domestic interest rates," Mohr said.

South Africa's economic problems should not be exaggerated, Mohr said, with the deficit on the balance of payments standing at only three percent of gross domestic product, quite modest by international norms.
"The deficit only needs to be narrowed moderately, say to about half its present size, in order to match the present lower level of capital inflows," he said.
"This is in stark contrast with the painful experiences of the 1970s and 1980s, when larger deficits had to be turned into surpluses quickly, inducing deep recessions."
Mohr said the current account deficit would shrink, reflecting both the fall in the rand and high interest rates.

In the past these factors had always led to a rapid and significant improvement in the foreign trade position, although the recovery could be more gradual this time due to weak commodity prices and the cheapness of imported goods.
The bulk of the improvement in the balance of payments was only likely next year, he said.
Although inflation remained relatively low, the risks remain significant, he added.

"Continued strong money supply growth and substantial real wage increase are a potential threat to inflation over the medium term. To retain progress on lowering inflation, monetary policy needs to err on the side of caution."
Consumer price inflation rose to an annual 8.4 percent in September from 7.5 percent in August.
